author: manuelhfx
quote: I grew up with Grand Theft Auto. From the early top-down games onward, the appeal was never just the missions. It was the feeling that the city belonged to you: take a car, make a mess, get chased, find a way out, and create your own story between the objectives. GTA VI is an extraordinary technical achievement, but after playing it on Xbox Series X, I’m left wondering whether Rockstar still understands that particular kind of fun.Leonida is stunning. The streets, people, interiors and background activity create a world with an absurd level of detail. But a world can feel alive and still feel restrictive. Too often, I’m moving through a carefully staged sequence of errands, tutorials and relationship beats instead of being let loose in a crime sandbox. The game is full of things to do, but many of them feel like chores dressed up as immersion.Stealing a car is a good example. It has always been one of GTA’s most basic pleasures: spot a vehicle, take it, improvise. Here, getting the car you want can involve breaking in, hot-wiring it and dealing with alarms or other extra systems. I understand the idea: make theft feel more believable and give different cars different risks. In practice, it adds friction to an action that used to feel immediate and mischievous. Realism is only an improvement when it makes the play more fun. Here, it often makes the fun **** same issue appears in the small rules of daily life. You can leave the house in swimwear, but apparently not in underwear or nightwear. At first, I thought it was a glitch. Then I found out it was intentional. That’s the sort of detail that makes me question what this game means by realism. The world can simulate an astonishing amount, yet it draws a firm line at walking outside in pajamas. Why? It doesn’t make the game more believable to me; it makes it feel like I’m being managed by a set of arbitrary **** relationship between Jason and Lucia is central, and the game asks me to invest in it through shared activities and domestic details. That may work for players who want a crime story built around a couple. I don’t. I felt tethered to their relationship when I wanted the freedom to define my own experience in the city. Instead of feeling like a criminal making choices, I often felt like an audience member being guided through a story about two characters whose priorities I didn’t share.Then there’s the strange question of what the game considers acceptable chaos. You can kill people in places like a parade or a gay bar, yet other parts of the criminal fantasy feel increasingly managed and procedural. That doesn’t come across as bold or transgressive to me. It feels arbitrary: the game will let you do something shocking, but it doesn’t consistently give you the playful, unpredictable freedom that made those acts part of a wider sandbox. Shock value isn’t the same as agency.Even the spectacle can feel oddly restrained. I expect planes to be part of the same unpredictable physics toybox as cars and helicopters, where a bad decision can turn into a spectacular disaster. Instead, the experience can feel protected from the kind of absurd collision and escalation that older GTA players learned to create for themselves. The series used to thrive on the gap between what the game expected and what the player decided to do. GTA VI often feels like it has already decided how the moment should go.I can see the craft everywhere. The city is gorgeous, the performances are strong, and the systems are ambitious. I can also see why people will love the density, the realism and the focus on Jason and Lucia. But those strengths don’t fix the central problem for me: the game seems more interested in simulating a believable life than giving me the liberating, ridiculous crime fantasy I came here for.I don’t need every GTA to be a copy of the first games. I do need it to remember why those games were exciting. A huge map, thousands of details and elaborate systems don’t add up to freedom if the moment-to-moment play feels like a set of chores with occasional permission to cause mayhem.I grew up with GTA because it made me feel like anything could happen. In GTA VI, I keep feeling like the game has a preferred way for everything to **** this a GTA? It looks like one. It has the name, the city and the crime. But for me, the freedom that made GTA feel like GTA is buried under all the things it wants me to do.
